Notes: 2 Maccabees 12:29-31: during Judas Maccabee's campaign in Gilead (c. 163 BCE) his force came to Scythopolis, 'the Jews who dwelt there' testified to the goodwill and kind treatment shown them by the people of Scythopolis, so Judas did not attack and went up to Jerusalem for Shavuot. Earliest documented Jewish presence at Scythopolis in the Second Temple period; a resident Jewish community living among a gentile (Greek) majority, size not stated. YEAR ESTABLISHED basis (-950): earliest Israelite presence at the site - by Solomon's time (c. 970-931 BCE, midpoint -950) Beth-shean was part of Solomon's fifth administrative district under Baana son of Ahilud (1 Kings 4:12), per Encyclopaedia Judaica and the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia; the Israelite town was destroyed c. 733/2 BCE and the site resettled only in the 3rd c. BCE.

Hasmonean conquest: during the siege of Samaria by John Hyrcanus' sons Antigonus and Aristobulus, the Seleucid commander Epicrates 'openly betrayed Scythopolis, and other places near it, to the Jews' (Josephus, Antiquities 13.280). Beginning of Hasmonean (Jewish) rule over the city; date c. 108/107 BCE per modern scholarship. No figure for Jewish settlers.

Archaeology of the Hasmonean conquest: the Hellenistic town of Nysa on Tell Iztabba (re-founded by Antiochus IV) was conquered and destroyed by John Hyrcanus in 108/07 BCE, who 'sent its inhabitants into exile'; the town was rebuilt only under Pompey. Event marking the end of the gentile Seleucid town; the source says nothing about Jewish settlers.

Megillat Ta'anit, 15-16 Sivan: 'the people of Bethshean {Scythopolis} and the valley were exiled' - a Hasmonean victory day commemorating the expulsion of the gentile inhabitants (dated c. 107 BCE by association with the Hasmonean conquest; the scroll itself gives no year). Event; Jewish population not stated.

Per this reference overview: John Hyrcanus I secured possession of Scythopolis in 107 BCE; the inhabitants were 'given the choice of converting to Judaism or leaving, most of the inhabitants left.' Hasmonean Judaization event; no Jewish population figure.

Josephus, Antiquities 13.395-397: at the end of Alexander Jannaeus' reign (d. 76 BCE; c.) Scythopolis is listed among the cities 'possessed' by the Jews (with Mount Carmel, Mount Tabor and Gadara, 'near the country of Samaria'). Documents continued Hasmonean/Jewish control of the city; no population figure.

Josephus, Antiquities 14.75: after his conquest of Judaea (63 BCE) Pompey 'restored the rest of the cities, Hippos, and Scythopolis, and Pella...' to their own inhabitants, ending Jewish rule; Scythopolis became a city of the Decapolis. Event; fate of the city's Jews not stated.

Josephus, Antiquities 14.88: under the proconsul Gabinius (57-55 BCE; c. 57) Scythopolis was rebuilt together with Samaria, Ashdod, Anthedon, Raphia and Dora, so that 'these cities were securely inhabited, which had been desolate for a long time.' Re-foundation of the city as a gentile polis; no statement about Jews.

Grossmark (2023): 'It is difficult to assess the situation of the Jews of the city in the Hasmonean period, or at the beginning of the Roman period, after Gabinius's settlements'; G. Fuks relied on M. Avi-Yonah (1962), who assumed the city's Jewish inhabitants were expelled to make way for a Hellenistic population (also Kasher 1988). This is a scholarly assumption, not documented absence, so Population left blank. (Cited from the open-access PDF of the Mazor Festschrift, Archaeopress 2023, chapter by T. Grossmark, p. 33-34; text extracted locally.)

Grossmark (2023), citing Fuks 1983: 149 n. 11: about thirty Jewish ossuaries were uncovered in the city's northern cemetery by the Philadelphia (University of Pennsylvania) expedition in the early 20th century, all with Greek inscriptions (never published) - evidence of a Hellenized resident Jewish community in the late Second Temple period. Dated by the source to the period before the Great Revolt; year is the midpoint of the 1st c. CE (=50), c.

Grossmark (2023): 'On the eve of the Great Revolt, the Jewish population of Beth She'an apparently numbered several thousand souls.' No precise figure, so Population left blank. She adds that Josephus' figure of over 13,000 Jews of Beth She'an murdered (War 2.18.3) 'almost certainly exaggerated the number of victims' (Broshi 1982: 23). Scale: a substantial minority community of several thousand in a gentile polis.

Josephus, War 2.458 and 2.466-468: after the massacre at Caesarea (66 CE) Jewish rebels laid waste Scythopolis; the Jews of Scythopolis fought alongside the citizens against the raiders, then were ordered out of the city with their families to a neighbouring grove, where on the third night the Scythopolitans killed them: 'The number that was slain was above thirteen thousand.' Ancient death-toll figure (scholars consider it exaggerated) - Population blank. Massacre of the resident Jewish community; War 2.477 refers to 'this murder at Scythopolis'; War 7.364-365 (Eleazar's speech at Masada) recalls it again.

Josephus, War 2.469-476: Simon son of Saul, 'a man of reputation among the Jews', a Jewish resident of Scythopolis who had fought against the Jewish attackers, killed his father, mother, wife and children and then himself in the grove when the Scythopolitans attacked (66 CE). Named Jewish resident family; presence row.

Josephus, Life 25-26: the inhabitants of Scythopolis forced the Jews living among them to bear arms against their countrymen and, after the victory, 'slew them all, being in number many ten thousands' (the translation adds [13,000] in brackets). Ancient death-toll figure, exaggerated per modern scholars - Population blank. Josephus claims all were killed, but because the figures are rhetorical and the source does not state that no Jews remained, Population is not entered as 0.
